canonical_implementation_steps.do: Publish only pre-approved AI models, services, and tools as AWS Service Catalog products in curated portfolios, and apply the launch constraint to EVERY product individually — a launch constraint does NOT apply at the portfolio level, nor to a product across all portfolios, so any product published without its own constraint is simply unconstrained — plus IAM-scoped access to the portfolio.

controls.canonical_question: Is AI service spend attributable to the team, workload, and environment that created it, through activated cost-allocation tags that resources cannot be created without?
controls.canonical_guidance: Two halves, both required: the tags are ACTIVATED as cost-allocation tags in the management account's billing settings (activation is a billing-console action — a tag on a resource is invisible to Cost Explorer until activated), and a tag policy on the AI OU prevents untagged or wrongly-valued resources being created. Check Billing > Cost allocation tags for active status, and Organizations > Policies > Tag policies for enforcement on the AI OU.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Attribution is the prerequisite for every other cost control: without it a budget or anomaly monitor can only be scoped to a whole account, so a shared account's runaway agent is indistinguishable from normal growth. Agree a minimal tag set (team, workload, environment, and where it is knowable model-id or agent-id), then ACTIVATE those keys as cost-allocation tags in the management account (Billing > Cost allocation tags) — user-defined tags are inert for cost reporting until activated, it can take up to 24 hours for a tag to appear in the billing console and up to a further 24 hours for activation to take effect, so do it before the spend you want to analyze.

controls.canonical_question: Are the security services that monitor AI workloads administered from a dedicated security-tooling account designated as delegated administrator, rather than from the organization management account?
controls.canonical_guidance: Check each service's admin account: Security Hub CSPM, GuardDuty, AWS Config (aggregator + conformance packs), Amazon Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer and Firewall Manager all support a delegated administrator. Verify the SAME account is the admin for each -- the administrator-member relationship does NOT propagate between services, so a per-service check is required. Confirm via organizations list-delegated-administrators and each service's own get-administrator-account / describe-organization-configuration call.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Designate a dedicated security-tooling account as delegated administrator for every security service that supports one, and keep the management account out of day-to-day security operations -- an operator working findings there is working in the account that can alter SCPs, Organizations and billing, which is the widest possible blast radius.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Per the AWS Security Reference Architecture this is the Security Tooling account, paired with a Log Archive account for immutable centralized logging; both are foundational accounts distinct from the AI workload accounts.

controls.canonical_question: Is there a single, current inventory of all AI models, agents, and AI-enabled applications in use across the organization?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for a maintained registry/catalog covering owner, purpose, and status for each AI workload; ad hoc spreadsheets that go stale don't count.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Work up the tiers rather than starting at the most complex. TIER 1, least effort: enable AWS Security Hub AI inventory, which continuously discovers AI assets across the organization from the delegated-administrator account.

src.t: AI inventory in AWS Security Hub (discovery sources and supported resources)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Know its boundary before you rely on it: managed discovery reads AWS Config configuration items, so AWS Config must be enabled in every account and Region you expect to see, and it covers a supported subset of Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon SageMaker resource types.

src.t: AI inventory in AWS Security Hub (discovery sources and supported resources)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Self-hosted models and third-party AI services are not discovered as resources at all -- they surface only indirectly, from Amazon Inspector SBOM findings for AI/ML packages and Amazon GuardDuty DNS activity to AI service domains.

src.t: AI inventory in AWS Security Hub (discovery sources and supported resources)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: So TIER 1 is the fastest start and the authoritative view of managed AWS AI resources, not a complete answer to this control: everything outside those sources still has to be registered deliberately.

controls.canonical_question: Can access to break-glass or emergency-override procedures for AI workloads be exercised without bypassing normal approval and logging controls?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm emergency-access paths (e.g., disabling a guardrail) are logged and require secondary approval, not an unmonitored superuser path.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Two different mechanisms are needed here and they are routinely conflated. (1) An override you can still exercise when the normal path is DOWN: the IAM Identity Center emergency (break-glass) access configuration -- a dedicated emergency-operations account with direct SAML 2.0 federation to the IdP that bypasses Identity Center, plus an emergency-operations group carrying no standing members, populated only during an incident.

src.t: Emergency access configuration for IAM Identity Center (business continuity)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Be clear what AWS designed this for: continuity during a disruption of the IdP, of a Region, or of IAM Identity Center itself. It is not an approval gate, and it deliberately has no approver in the loop.

src.t: Emergency access configuration for IAM Identity Center (business continuity)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: (2) The approval gate this control actually asks about -- request, approve, time-bound grant, automatic expiry, for an action such as disabling a guardrail: temporary elevated access, also called just-in-time access.

src.t: Temporary elevated access (just-in-time) with IAM Identity Center

canonical_implementation_steps.do: There is NO native Identity Center setting that provides it; AWS documents temporary elevated access as delivered either by a validated partner solution (Apono, CyberArk, Okta Access Requests, Tenable) or by something you build on Identity Center APIs, so name the mechanism you actually run rather than assuming the platform supplies one.

src.t: Temporary elevated access (just-in-time) with IAM Identity Center

canonical_implementation_steps.do: The control passes only if both halves hold: every assumption of an elevated or emergency role lands in CloudTrail in the target account, and the grant expires on its own rather than being revoked from memory.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Leverage the per-account/OU isolation to quarantine a single workload without wider outage: attach a targeted Deny SCP or IAM policy to that account, revoke the workload role's active sessions (the IAM Revoke active sessions capability / an aws:TokenIssueTime deny condition), and stop the specific Bedrock or SageMaker resource.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Know the one exception before you rely on session revocation: you cannot revoke the active session of a service-linked role, so a workload that acts through one has to be stopped at the resource.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: THREE THINGS THAT MAKE THIS NOT A LOCKOUT UNLESS YOU BUILD IT THAT WAY. (1) Revoking sessions does not stop re-entry: the policy denies credentials issued before now 'as well as approximately 30 seconds into the future' to cover propagation delay, and 'if the user assumes the role after you revoked the permissions, then the deny policy does not apply to that user' — anyone still holding sts:AssumeRole on that role simply re-assumes it half a minute later.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Revocation has to be paired in the same runbook step with removing the ability to assume (tighten the trust policy or pull the identity's AssumeRole grant), and note you cannot revoke the session of a service-linked role at all.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: (2) This path does not work on IAM Identity Center principals, because 'you can't edit roles in IAM that were created from IAM Identity Center permission sets'.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: AWS's documented mechanism there is a Deny-all policy conditioned on identitystore:userId, pre-deployed as an SCP with an invalid placeholder user ID across every account the workforce can reach and edited to the real user ID during the incident — 'the recommended approach for its ease and speed of impact', and only fast because the deployment already happened, so pre-deploying it IS the runbook step.

controls.required_proof: Signing key per trust zone + a receiving agent rejecting a message that fails Verify
controls.canonical_question: Are messages between agents signed by the sender and verified by the receiver at the message level, so a receiving agent proves who sent an instruction and that its content is unmodified, rather than trusting the transport alone?
controls.canonical_guidance: Distinct from TLS and from caller authentication (AIR-FND-IAM-08), and distinct from an authenticated channel (AIR-ACR-RT-07, AIR-SLF-AGT-05): those protect the message in flight, and an asynchronous multi-agent workflow leaves it at rest in a queue or event bus where there is no channel left to trust. Look for the sender signing the serialized payload with a KMS asymmetric key, the signature traveling with the message as message metadata so it survives every intermediary, the receiver calling Verify and rejecting before it acts, and one signing key per trust zone rather than one key shared by every agent. Check the at-rest half too: SSE on the inter-agent queues with a customer-managed key per zone.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Provision one AWS KMS asymmetric key pair per agent trust zone for message signing, choosing a signing key spec (RSA or ECC) rather than an encryption spec, so a key compromise in one zone cannot forge messages in another.

src.t: Choosing a KMS key spec — RSA and ECC signing specs, and which usages each supports
Key policies — scoping kms:Sign to the sending agent's role and kms:Verify to the receivers

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Have the sending agent sign the serialized message payload with the KMS Sign API and attach the signature plus the signing key ARN as message attributes, so the signature travels with the payload through every queue, topic, and event bus rather than terminating at the transport.

src.t: KMS Sign — producing a signature over the message payload
SQS message attributes — structured metadata carried alongside the message body

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Have the receiving agent call the KMS Verify API and reject the message before any instruction in it is acted on, so a forged or tampered payload never reaches the agent's reasoning loop; treat a verification failure as a security event, not a parse error.

src.t: KMS Verify — verifying the signature and the signing key before trusting the payload

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Enable SQS server-side encryption with a customer-managed KMS key on every queue carrying inter-agent messages, using a separate key per trust zone so at-rest exposure is bounded to one zone; existing queues can be converted in place.

src.t: SQS server-side encryption with a customer managed KMS key
Configuring SSE on an existing queue

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Keep signing key ARNs in Parameter Store rather than in agent code, and rotate the signing keys manually on a schedule — AWS KMS automatic and on-demand rotation cover symmetric encryption keys only, and name asymmetric and HMAC keys as requiring manual rotation, so plan an overlap window in which receivers still accept signatures from the outgoing key.

src.t: Rotating KMS keys — manual rotation is required for asymmetric and HMAC keys
Parameter Store — holding the current and previous signing key ARNs outside the code

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Alarm on signing-key usage anomalies in CloudWatch — kms:Sign called by a role that should only verify, or a sudden rise in signing volume from one agent — because a stolen signing capability is otherwise indistinguishable from normal traffic.

src.t: CloudWatch alarms on a metric or metric math expression

canonical_implementation_steps.do: For agents on AgentCore Runtime using the A2A protocol, layer message-level signing on top of A2A's own authentication for any exchange that crosses a trust boundary: A2A authenticates the calling agent, which is a statement about the connection rather than about a payload that outlives it.

src.t: Agent-to-agent (A2A) protocol support in AgentCore Runtime

controls.canonical_question: Is sensitive data (PII, PHI, financial, or classified) discovered and classified before it is used as AI input, training data, or grounding context?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for automated or process-driven classification/discovery that runs before data reaches a model or knowledge base, not just after-the-fact audits.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Use both Macie mechanisms, because they answer different questions and are not interchangeable. Amazon Macie automated sensitive-data discovery continually evaluates your S3 inventory but selects representative objects by SAMPLING, so it gives estate-wide sensitivity visibility and tells you where to look — it is not per-object assurance over the specific set about to be ingested, and it is per-Region over general purpose buckets.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Run a targeted sensitive-data discovery job (managed plus custom data identifiers) over the actual AI source prefixes to get that assurance, and treat the automated map as what prioritizes which prefixes need one.

controls.canonical_question: Are backups or snapshots of AI training data and model artifacts protected against tampering or deletion, including by a compromised administrator?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for immutability (e.g., object lock, versioning with deletion protection) on backups of training data and model artifacts.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Store backups of training data and model artifacts in S3 with Object Lock in Compliance mode (WORM) plus versioning, and lock AWS Backup vaults with Vault Lock in Compliance mode.

src.t: Locking objects with S3 Object Lock
AWS Backup Vault Lock — vault lock modes and grace time

canonical_implementation_steps.do: In Compliance mode neither an IAM principal nor the account root can alter or delete recovery points before the retention period expires, protecting against a compromised administrator.

src.t: AWS Backup Vault Lock — vault lock modes and grace time

canonical_implementation_steps.do: TWO WAYS A COMPLIANCE-MODE VAULT LOCK IS WEAKER THAN IT READS, both of which leave the compromised-administrator window this control names still open. First, a Compliance-mode lock is immutable only after its grace time expires — you choose the grace time and it must be at least 3 days (72 hours), and AWS states that during grace time you can still remove the vault lock and change its configuration, so a lock created today is administrator-removable for at least the next three days.

src.t: AWS Backup Vault Lock — vault lock modes and grace time

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Track the lock's start date, not just its mode.

src.t: AWS Backup Vault Lock — vault lock modes and grace time

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Second, PutBackupVaultLockConfiguration selects the mode by the presence of one parameter: include ChangeableForDays and you get Compliance mode, omit it and you silently get Governance mode, which AWS documents as removable by any user with sufficient IAM permissions.

src.t: AWS Backup Vault Lock — vault lock modes and grace time

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Assert the mode from the vault's returned lock configuration rather than from the call you believe you made.

src.t: AWS Backup Vault Lock — vault lock modes and grace time

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Note also that the lock's minimum and maximum retention periods do not apply retroactively — recovery points already in the vault keep their previous lifecycle settings.

controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm a written retention policy exists specifying how long AI interaction data is kept and when it should be deleted.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Define a written retention and deletion schedule for prompts, model outputs, and conversation history, then bind it to an enforceable control by encoding the period as Amazon S3 Lifecycle expiration rules on the storage buckets (and equivalent TTLs on any DynamoDB or CloudWatch Logs stores) so the documented period maps to a technical mechanism, not just intent.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: THE SCHEDULE MUST ALSO COVER THE MODEL'S OWN RETENTION, NOT ONLY YOUR COPIES. Amazon Bedrock retains prompts and outputs according to a data-retention mode resolved as 'first non-inherit value of (project -> account -> model default)', and inherit is the default for new accounts and projects — so an account nobody has configured has made no retention decision and each model's built-in default governs.

src.t: Data retention (Amazon Bedrock)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Under default mode AWS states it may retain the data for safety and abuse-prevention purposes, and on the Responses API store=false 'does not guarantee zero data retention'.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Set the account mode explicitly with PutAccountDataRetention (mode none for zero retention, which writes no request or response data to durable storage), set it per project where projects are used, and read back each model's effective mode and allowed_modes rather than assuming — if your effective mode is outside a model's allowed_modes that model reports status unavailable and its requests are blocked, so this is an availability decision as well as a retention one.

controls.canonical_question: Is the data-retention and deletion schedule for AI interaction data actually enforced, with deletion occurring automatically on schedule?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm deletion actually happens on the defined schedule (e.g., automated lifecycle/expiry), not just that a policy is written down.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Enforce the schedule with S3 Lifecycle configuration Expiration actions (plus NoncurrentVersionExpiration on versioned buckets), which Amazon S3 evaluates daily to automatically delete expired objects.

src.t: Expiring objects — S3 Lifecycle expiration considerations

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Confirm enforcement from an S3 Lifecycle Event Notification for an object that actually expired rather than from the lifecycle rule's status, because a present, Enabled rule is not evidence that anything was deleted.

src.t: S3 Lifecycle event notifications

canonical_implementation_steps.do: NoncurrentVersionExpiration is not optional on a versioned bucket: on a versioning-enabled bucket an Expiration action on the current version only adds a delete marker, and AWS states object expiration 'applies only to an object's current version (it has no impact on noncurrent object versions)' — so an Expiration rule alone retains every prior version of every prompt and output indefinitely while presenting as enforced.

src.t: Expiring objects — S3 Lifecycle expiration considerations

canonical_implementation_steps.do: FOUR DOCUMENTED CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH EXPIRATION SILENTLY DOES NOTHING, each of which reads as compliant: Amazon S3 'doesn't take any action on noncurrent versions of objects that have the S3 Object Lock configuration applied' — which collides directly with AIR-FND-DAT-05, since applying Object Lock in Compliance mode to the same data this control expires means the expiration will not run.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: S3 takes no action when one or more versions exist and a delete marker is already the current version.

src.t: Expiring objects — S3 Lifecycle expiration considerations

canonical_implementation_steps.do: S3 takes no action on current or noncurrent versions of objects whose replication status is Pending or Failed.

src.t: Expiring objects — S3 Lifecycle expiration considerations

canonical_implementation_steps.do: For a tag-based filter S3 re-evaluates the object's tags at execution time, so removing the triggering tag after the action is queued cancels the expiration.

controls.canonical_question: When an AI system is deprecated or a model is retired, is there a defined process to securely dispose of the associated training data, artifacts, and credentials?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for a decommissioning checklist covering data deletion, credential revocation, and artifact disposal for retired AI systems.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Maintain a decommissioning checklist that on retirement deletes S3 data and artifacts (lifecycle or explicit delete), revokes the IAM roles/access keys and Secrets Manager secrets, and calls KMS ScheduleKeyDeletion on the data-specific customer-managed key so remaining ciphertext becomes cryptographically unrecoverable (crypto-shredding); retain the completed record as evidence.

src.t: Delete an AWS KMS key
ScheduleKeyDeletion — PendingWindowInDays
Delete an AWS Secrets Manager secret

canonical_implementation_steps.do: NEITHER DELETION IS IMMEDIATE, SO DO NOT CLOSE THE RECORD ON THE API CALL: ScheduleKeyDeletion takes a PendingWindowInDays of 7-30 days (default 30), the actual deletion can land up to 24 hours later than the scheduled date, and CancelKeyDeletion can recover the key for the whole window.

src.t: ScheduleKeyDeletion — PendingWindowInDays
Delete an AWS KMS key

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Secrets Manager likewise 'does not immediately delete secrets' but schedules them after a recovery window of a minimum of seven days.

src.t: Delete an AWS Secrets Manager secret

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Take the closing evidence from the CloudTrail DeleteKey event, not the ScheduleKeyDeletion event.

src.t: Delete an AWS KMS key

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Scheduling deletion also 'might not immediately affect data keys encrypted by the KMS key', so a process already holding a decrypted data key keeps reading.

src.t: Delete an AWS KMS key

canonical_implementation_steps.do: THREE DOCUMENTED CASES WHERE THE DELETE SHREDS NOTHING: (1) a multi-Region REPLICA key is reversible — 'You can delete a replica key at any time' and 'if you mistakenly delete a replica key, you can recreate it by replicating the same primary key in the same Region' — so where AI data was replicated across Regions you must schedule every replica and then the primary, whose waiting period only begins when the last replica is deleted.

src.t: Delete an AWS KMS key

canonical_implementation_steps.do: (2) DeleteImportedKeyMaterial is 'temporary and reversible' because the material can be reimported, so a runbook step reading 'delete the key material' has not shredded anything.

src.t: DeleteImportedKeyMaterial — temporary and reversible
Delete an AWS KMS key

canonical_implementation_steps.do: (3) a replicated secret cannot be deleted at all until its replicas are — 'you can't delete a primary secret if it is replicated to other Regions'.

src.t: Delete an AWS Secrets Manager secret

canonical_implementation_steps.do: The unrecoverability the checklist depends on is guaranteed for a deleted single-Region symmetric encryption key, where metadata unique to that key is cryptographically bound to each ciphertext, so even the identical key material reimported into a new key cannot decrypt it.

src.t: Delete an AWS KMS key

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Order the checklist to revoke before it shreds: deleting a secret makes it inaccessible immediately even though disposal completes later, and for an asymmetric ENCRYPT_DECRYPT key the public key may already be outside AWS KMS, where 'alarms, logs, and other strategies that detect attempted use of KMS key that is pending deletion cannot detect use of the public key' — so check CloudTrail for public-key downloads as part of retirement rather than assuming the key policy bounded it.

controls.canonical_question: Is every AI workload whose data must remain inaccessible to its own operating environment identified, with decryption bound to an attested enclave measurement rather than to an IAM principal alone?
controls.canonical_guidance: For the highest-sensitivity inference or training, an IAM-authorized role is still a role a compromised host can use. Start by confirming the identification exists and covers every AI workload, then — for each one it placed in scope — that the KMS key policy releases the key only against a verified measurement — so decryption fails on an unmeasured or debug environment even with valid IAM permissions. Read the whole key policy, not just the statement carrying the condition: attestation binds that statement, so any other statement allowing the same actions unconditioned is a second, unattested path to the same plaintext, and it looks identical in a policy excerpt. A workload that has no such data satisfies this control on the identification alone: the empty set is a legitimate Yes, and the recorded determination — which data classes were considered, and why none of them requires host-inaccessibility — is the evidence for it. That is deliberately not a separate answer state; leaving the control unanswered instead reads as review that has not happened yet, and answering Yes without the determination asserts a scoping decision nobody made.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: PIN DEPLOYMENT CONTEXT, NOT JUST THE IMAGE: the EIF is not a secret, so PCR0/ImageSha384 alone is satisfied by the same image rebuilt and launched anywhere by anyone holding the Principal's credentials — add PCR3 (parent IAM role) or PCR4 (parent instance ID), with AWS recommending PCR3 plus PCR8 (signing certificate) together 'for the best flexibility'; PCR1 (kernel/bootstrap) and PCR2 (application) add image integrity but no deployment binding.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: You generate those two yourself as a SHA384 of the parent's IAM role ARN or its instance ID, padded with 48 null bytes, so a padding or ARN-format mistake produces a hash that can never match and presents as a broken deployment rather than as a policy error; and although the condition key accepts PCR0 through PCR31, a condition on any index outside those six can never be satisfied either.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Force outbound traffic through AWS Network Firewall stateful domain allow-list rule groups, matching TLS_SNI for HTTPS and the HTTP host header for HTTP.

src.t: Stateful rule groups with domain lists (Allow default drop, HOME_NET, SNI matching)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: The Allow action supplies the default drop itself — traffic of the inspected protocol that does not match the domain specifications is denied — so do not also attach Reject or Alert domain rule groups to a policy that uses default action ordering, where that implicit drop is evaluated before your other rules.

src.t: Stateful rule groups with domain lists (Allow default drop, HOME_NET, SNI matching)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Set the HOME_NET rule variable to cover every CIDR you want inspected: domain-list inspection defaults to traffic originating inside the firewall's own VPC, so traffic arriving from other VPCs or on-premises is not inspected until you widen it.

src.t: Stateful rule groups with domain lists (Allow default drop, HOME_NET, SNI matching)

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Pair this with Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall allow-list rule groups and treat that pairing as required rather than defense in depth: DNS queries sent to the Route 53 Resolver are routed to a static address in the VPC and are therefore not inspected by Network Firewall at all, including by the AWS managed rule groups, and security groups cannot block them either.

src.t: AWS managed rule groups disclaimer — Route 53 Resolver DNS queries are not inspected
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Keep the two domain lists in sync, end the DNS Firewall rule group with an explicit BLOCK on * so anything off the list fails to resolve, and restrict security-group egress to the required ports.

src.t: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Add IP and CIDR rules alongside the domain rules on your highest-value paths, because Network Firewall does not pause connections to perform out-of-band DNS lookups — it matches on the SNI or host header the client presents, not the address it actually connects to, so a client offering an approved SNI while connecting elsewhere passes the domain allow-list.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Front public AI endpoints (API Gateway, ALB, or CloudFront) with an AWS WAF web ACL using the SQL injection and XSS attack rule statements plus rate-based rules, and set the SQLi sensitivity level to HIGH — it defaults to LOW, while AWS documents HIGH as detecting more SQL injection attacks and as the recommended setting.

Using rate-based rule statements in AWS WAF

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Then fix the limit that quietly decides whether inspection reaches an AI request at all: AWS WAF inspects the request body only up to a per-resource-type ceiling — fixed at 8 KB for Application Load Balancer and AppSync, and defaulting to 16 KB (raisable in 16 KB increments to 64 KB) for CloudFront, API Gateway, Amazon Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

src.t: Managing body inspection size limits in AWS WAF

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Prompt bodies routinely exceed 8 KB, and the default OversizeHandling is CONTINUE, which inspects only the portion within the limit and forwards the request, so an oversized prompt passes the injection rules uninspected.

src.t: Managing body inspection size limits in AWS WAF

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Raise the limit where the resource type allows it and choose OversizeHandling deliberately (MATCH to treat oversize as a hit, or NO_MATCH with a separate size-constraint rule) rather than leaving the default; note gRPC bodies cannot be inspected.

controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm distinct AI workloads (e.g., different agents or applications) are placed in separate network segments with controlled paths between them, not a single flat network.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Segment distinct AI workloads into separate subnets, VPCs or accounts so a compromise of one cannot reach another's segment, and route required cross-segment traffic through a Transit Gateway or PrivateLink with a Network Firewall inspection VPC.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Then pick the enforcement mechanism per path, because security-group referencing does not work everywhere the segmentation does, and a rule that silently never matches reads as a control while enforcing nothing.

src.t: Security group rules — referencing scope and the middlebox limitation

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Referencing a peer security group works in an inbound rule when the groups are in the same VPC, across a VPC peering connection, or across a transit gateway — but in an outbound rule only for the same VPC or a peering connection, not across a transit gateway.

src.t: Security group rules — referencing scope and the middlebox limitation

canonical_implementation_steps.do: It is not supported across transit gateway peering connections at all (both VPCs must attach to the same transit gateway, which rules out the cross-Region case), and not supported for PrivateLink endpoints, where AWS recommends IP CIDR-based rules instead.

src.t: Transit gateway VPC attachments — security group referencing limitations

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Most importantly for the inspection path this control prescribes: if you route traffic between instances in different subnets through a middlebox appliance, each security group must reference the other instance's private IP or its subnet CIDR — referencing the other instance's security group as the source does not allow the traffic to flow — and referencing through a transit gateway does not work across a Gateway Load Balancer or AWS Network Firewall.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: So use peer security-group references for same-VPC and peered paths, and CIDR-based rules plus subnet network ACLs for transit-gateway, PrivateLink and inspected paths.

controls.canonical_question: Are internet-facing entry points to AI workloads protected against volumetric and application-layer DDoS attacks, rather than relying on the always-on baseline protection alone?
controls.canonical_guidance: Check for an explicit, configured L7 mitigation on the AI entry point — not the always-on baseline. AWS Shield Standard applies to every customer at no cost and needs no configuration, so its presence is already true of an unprotected account and proves nothing here. The current mechanism is the AWS WAF Anti-DDoS managed rule group (AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet, 50 WCUs): confirm it is referenced in the web ACL associated with the entry point, and check the Block and Challenge sensitivity levels are set deliberately rather than left at defaults, since they tune independently. Note this does NOT require a Shield Advanced subscription — any AWS WAF customer can enable it — so absence of Shield Advanced is not an excuse for absence of this control. If you find Shield Advanced automatic application-layer mitigation (L7AM) instead, that is the legacy path: it was superseded by the managed rule group on 2026-03-26 and is available to new subscribers only via AWS Support, so treat it as Partial and plan the migration. Where Shield Advanced IS subscribed, verify per-resource enrollment too: CreateProtection accepts only a CloudFront distribution, Route 53 hosted zone, Global Accelerator standard accelerator, Elastic IP, Application Load Balancer or Classic Load Balancer — an EC2 instance or Network Load Balancer is protected only by association with a protected Elastic IP, so look for that association rather than the instance itself. API Gateway and Lambda function URLs are not Shield Advanced resource types, so the protectable edge is a CloudFront distribution in front of them. Finally, confirm a request-rate cap exists on the inference path specifically, because the distinctive loss on an AI endpoint is token and inference spend as much as availability.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Add the AWS WAF Anti-DDoS managed rule group (AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet, 50 WCUs) to the web ACL on every internet-facing AI entry point, and set the Block and Challenge sensitivity levels deliberately — they tune independently, so you can run Challenge at high sensitivity to catch more suspicious traffic while keeping Block low to avoid dropping legitimate requests.

controls.canonical_question: Is the audit trail that records agent and model activity protected against tampering, deletion, and retention-shortening — including by a compromised account administrator — where it actually lives, in CloudWatch Logs as well as CloudTrail?
controls.canonical_guidance: Most of the substantive agent audit record — input/output prompts, reasoning traces, tool invocations, session spans, and AgentCore Memory data-plane events — is delivered to CloudWatch Log groups, not CloudTrail, and CloudWatch Logs has no S3-style object lock. Individual log events are already append-only; the realistic tamper vectors are deleting the log group/stream or shortening retention. Look for log-group deletion protection, an SCP restricting delete/retention actions to a named provisioning role, KMS encryption, and an authoritative copy forwarded to a separate log-archive account or WORM store.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Protect the agent audit trail where it actually lives. The substantive records — input/output prompts, reasoning traces, tool invocations, session spans, and AgentCore Memory data-plane events (CreateEvent/DeleteEvent/RetrieveMemoryRecords) — are delivered to CloudWatch Log groups (e.g. /aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/*, aws/spans, and Bedrock model-invocation log groups), which have no native WORM; log events are already append-only, so the real tamper vectors are deleting the log group or stream, shortening retention, disabling the protection itself, and cutting the forwarding path.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Two details decide whether that SCP works at all: DeleteLogStream authorizes on the log-stream ARN, so its Resource needs the log-group ARN plus a trailing :log-stream:* rather than the log-group ARN alone, and no logs action defines a service-specific condition key, so scope the provisioning-role exception on aws:PrincipalArn — a Deny conditioned on a key the action does not define never matches and fails open, granting exactly what it was written to block.

controls.canonical_question: Is adversarial and penetration testing of the agent run against a scoped test environment with its own credentials, memory store, and tool endpoints, rather than against the production agent?
controls.canonical_guidance: AIR-FND-DET-08 asks whether the testing happens; this asks where. An agent under test executes the exploit — it really calls the tool, really sends the message, really writes to memory — so an injection payload that lands in a shared memory store shapes a real user's answer later. Look for a documented in-scope and out-of-scope list per assessment, a test agent instance with its own memory store and tool endpoints, external dependencies mocked or sandboxed, test credentials held in Secrets Manager and rotated after each cycle rather than long-lived and shared, network and IAM segmentation that stops the test instance reaching production resources, and test logs landing in your own account.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Stand up a test environment that replicates the agent architecture with its own AgentCore Memory resource, its own tool endpoints, and its own permission boundaries, so an attack payload that succeeds cannot persist into the memory a production user's session retrieves.

controls.canonical_question: When an agent is contained automatically, is its state captured for forensics before its credentials are revoked, so the evidence needed to investigate survives the containment?
controls.canonical_guidance: AIR-FND-DET-07 asks whether containment is automatic and AIR-SLF-AGT-07 whether a credential kill-switch exists; this asks about the order of operations, which is where the evidence is lost. Look for an automation that snapshots the agent's current memory, active sessions, and pending operations to S3 first, then revokes credentials by attaching a deny-all policy to the agent's role while preserving the role itself for analysis, then broadcasts the quarantine event so dependent workflows trip their circuit breakers. Stopping the process first loses in-memory state; deleting the role destroys the forensic subject. Look too for restoration gated behind a runbook that needs more than one person, so a contained agent is not re-enabled before the investigation concludes.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Trigger containment from an EventBridge rule on the anomaly alarm into a single automation — a Lambda function or an SSM Automation runbook — so the ordering of the steps is a property of the automation rather than of whoever responds.

src.t: EventBridge rules — routing the anomaly event to the containment automation

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Make the first action the snapshot: write the agent's current memory contents, active session identifiers, and pending operations to S3, with Object Lock where the snapshot has to be defensible later, because none of that state survives the revocation that follows.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Only then revoke: attach a deny-all inline policy to the agent's role conditioned on aws:TokenIssueTime so existing sessions are invalidated, and keep the role in place — deleting it removes the very configuration the investigation needs to read.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Broadcast the quarantine as an EventBridge event so peer agents and orchestrating workflows route to their fallback paths rather than retrying a principal that will now deny everything.

controls.canonical_question: Is the queue of agent decisions awaiting human review prioritized by impact and monitored for backlog, per-reviewer load, and rubber-stamp indicators, rather than arriving as one undifferentiated stream?
controls.canonical_guidance: The failure mode is silent: a review gate that exists in the architecture and is rubber-stamped in practice scores the same as one that works. Look for review requests classified by impact — data sensitivity, reversibility, first time this agent has attempted the operation, time sensitivity — rather than first-in-first-out; alarms on backlog per priority tier, time-to-assignment, and time-to-decision; a cap on concurrent assignments per reviewer; and review-quality metrics (average review time, approval rate, reversal rate) watched for the short-review-time-with-high-approval-rate pattern that shows up when volume outruns attention.

controls.required_proof: Reviewer notification or screen showing the grounding/policy-check result, manipulation flags, and comparable past decisions
controls.canonical_question: When an agent action is routed to a human for approval, does the reviewer see signals independent of the agent — a grounding or policy-check result, manipulation-warning flags, and how this request compares with similar past ones — alongside the proposed action?
controls.canonical_guidance: Pair with AIR-FND-GOV-09: an approval gate with no context is the rubber-stamp anti-pattern in its purest form. Which signal is useful depends on the review's shape. Where the reviewer is judging whether the agent's recommendation is correct, the agent's own grounding score is informative. Where the reviewer is a policy gate on an action the agent has already committed to, the agent's self-reported confidence is close to worthless and the signal must come from something the agent does not author — a grounding or automated-reasoning check, anomaly detection, or the manipulation flags raised by input validation. Look for each number presented with a plain-language statement of what it means, and for similar past decisions surfaced so a first-of-its-kind request is visibly unusual.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Where the reviewer judges whether the agent is right, surface the Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding score with the request, and present it as a sentence about what it measures rather than a bare number — a reviewer who does not know what 0.7 means will treat every score as approval.

controls.required_proof: Marketplace/model-access control configuration
controls.canonical_question: Is there a technical control preventing use of unapproved third-party or marketplace models alongside first-party foundation models?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for allow-list enforcement that distinguishes approved first-party/marketplace models from anything a developer could otherwise enable.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Third-party Marketplace models (for example Anthropic Claude, Cohere, Stability AI) require an AWS Marketplace subscription, so restrict aws-marketplace:Subscribe, aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe, and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions via SCP/IAM — using the aws-marketplace:ProductId condition key to allow only approved product IDs — to stop developers self-enabling unapproved models.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Keep ProductId on the Allow side, as AWS's own example does, and do not build a Deny on it: the key is declared per-action only on AcceptAgreementRequest and CreateAgreementRequest in AWS's generated IAM service model, so a Deny conditioned on it may never match and would fail open, whereas an over-restrictive Allow fails closed and is visible.

controls.canonical_question: Is the compute capacity backing model inference isolated per workload or tenant, so one workload's usage cannot exhaust capacity needed by another?
controls.canonical_guidance: Check for provisioned throughput, dedicated capacity, or per-tenant quotas rather than a single shared pool with no isolation.

Virginia) and US West (Oregon)) or Provisioned Throughput, so reserve Provisioned Throughput for steady high-volume or latency-sensitive workloads.

controls.canonical_question: Are the production prompts that drive model behavior managed as controlled, versioned artifacts in a central catalog, rather than hardcoded ad hoc in application code?
controls.canonical_guidance: Prompts are executable logic: a changed system prompt can alter safety behavior or leak instructions. Confirm prompts are stored centrally, versioned with an immutable production snapshot, access-controlled, and encrypted — not free-floating strings edited inline and shipped without review.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Treat prompts as code artifacts — AWS prescriptive guidance for agentic AI BP 2.2 accepts either a managed prompt registry or Git-based prompt-as-code (a hybrid of the two is its advanced pattern), so pick one and govern it; Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management (BedrockAgent API, bedrock-agent-2023-06-05) is the managed-registry option and is what the rest of this recommendation describes.

controls.canonical_guidance: Agentic apps make many model and tool calls per request. canonical_implementation_steps.do: Use the agentic guardrail API, InvokeGuardrailChecks (POST /guardrail-checks/invoke, IAM action bedrock:InvokeGuardrailChecks), to apply inline safeguards at each step of the agent loop without creating a guardrail resource: it runs in detect-only mode, returning per-check severity/confidence scores (contentFilter VIOLENCE/HATE/SEXUAL/MISCONDUCT/INSULTS, promptAttack JAILBREAK/PROMPT_INJECTION/PROMPT_LEAKAGE, sensitiveInformation PII, up to 31 entity types) on the current messages so the caller enforces thresholds/actions and can add or drop checks per turn as the trajectory evolves.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Treat the embedding index as a derived copy of the source corpus at the same classification, because embedding inversion can partially reconstruct source text from vectors. controls.canonical_question: Does each agent session run in an isolated execution environment that does not leak state or data to unrelated sessions?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm one session cannot read or influence another's compute, memory, or filesystem. Note: if sessions share persistent storage (e.g. a mounted shared bucket), per-session isolation becomes the application's responsibility and must be enforced in code, not assumed from the runtime.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Know which compute type you are on, because the isolation guarantee differs. On the default serverless (microVM) compute, each SESSION runs in its own microVM with an isolated kernel, memory, and filesystem, and on session completion the microVM is terminated and its memory sanitized — so one session cannot read or influence another's compute.

src.t: How AgentCore Runtime works — dedicated microVM per session, terminated and memory sanitized on completion

canonical_implementation_steps.do: On AgentCore Instances (EC2 managed instances in your account) that guarantee does not hold between agents: AWS states agents on an instance are not isolated from each other, multiple agents can share the instance filesystem, and all agents sharing an instance must be mutually trusted — the SESSION is the isolation unit (capacity provider + session ID maps 1:1 to one instance), so use a separate capacity provider per trust boundary.

src.t: Security in AgentCore Instances — agents on an instance are not isolated from each other; the session is the isolation unit

canonical_implementation_steps.do: If sessions share persistent storage, prefer managed session storage, which the platform isolates per session (a session cannot read or write another session's storage, or any session of a different runtime), over a bring-your-own S3 Files or EFS mount.

src.t: Filesystem configurations — managed session storage is isolated per session

canonical_implementation_steps.do: A BYO mount CANNOT be narrowed per session: the access point's root directory and POSIX UID/GID are fixed in filesystemConfigurations and AgentCore mounts that same access point into every session at the configured path.

controls.canonical_question: Is invocation of the agent runtime restricted to an approved network path AND an approved caller, so neither the internet nor a direct call that bypasses the gateway can reach the agent?
controls.canonical_guidance: Two distinct restrictions, both on the runtime. Network: confirm the runtime is invoked only through its PrivateLink endpoint — Private DNS on, security group scoped to application SGs on 443, resource-based policy denying invocation unless it arrives via an approved VPC/VPC-endpoint, so a leaked credential alone cannot reach the agent from the internet. Caller: where a gateway fronts the runtime to apply policy, guardrails, and rate limits, confirm the runtime also rejects invocations that did not come from that gateway — otherwise a caller inside the approved VPC can invoke the runtime ARN directly and skip every gateway control.

controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm the gateway requires a validated identity on every inbound call (JWT from your IdP, or SigV4) and authorizes the caller itself — rather than trusting that the model would only ask for permitted things. All configured categories are checked; allowedScopes requires at least one matching configured scope. Test wrong issuer, expired token and mismatched configured audience/client/scope/custom claims, alongside a valid request.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Where a target needs per-user consent, only grantType AUTHORIZATION_CODE (3LO) does: a CLIENT_CREDENTIALS target is machine-to-machine, needs no consent, and never appears on a consent portal's Connections page, so reaching user-owned data through one is a finding rather than a configuration choice. On each AUTHORIZATION_CODE target served by a consent portal, set defaultReturnUrl to exactly <portalUrl>/connect/callback. A missing or wrong value does not fail closed: the outbound provider returns the user somewhere other than the portal and the consent never binds to the session, which is the cross-user grant this flow exists to prevent. Targets created BEFORE the portal existed carry a different defaultReturnUrl or none at all, so enumerate and update the pre-existing ones instead of only the new ones.

controls.canonical_guidance: AIR-ACR-MEM-01 covers encryption and partitioning, AIR-ACR-MEM-12 the audit trail of memory operations, and AIR-FND-DET-09 the tamper-proofing of that trail — none of them detects a record whose content was changed. Look for a keyed integrity tag computed over the record when it is written (KMS GenerateMac) and verified on read (VerifyMac) before the content enters the prompt, and for a verification failure that fails closed rather than logging and continuing.

controls.canonical_guidance: A Cedar condition is point-in-time: each request is judged alone, so an agent using permitted tools in an unintended order passes every individual check. Confirm the multi-step rules the workflow depends on are expressed as policy, and that their session scoping is understood: history is keyed to a caller-supplied session id, so these bound a looping or prompt-injected agent within a session, not a determined caller who can start a fresh one.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: AWS supports two deployment types and the choice changes what rollback you get: a BlueGreenUpdatePolicy (all-at-once, canary, or linear traffic shifting, with a baking period and termination-wait time) provisions a new fleet alongside the old one, so rollback is a traffic shift back to a fleet that is still running; a RollingUpdatePolicy replaces capacity in batches sized 5–50% of the fleet with its own baking period and auto-rollback, which costs less instance capacity but has no intact old fleet to shift back to mid-deployment.

controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm image scanning runs as a gate before deployment, with findings above an agreed severity blocking release. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) the image still lives in ECR, so check the registry-level configuration (`aws ecr get-registry-scanning-configuration`, expect `scanType: ENHANCED` with `CONTINUOUS_SCAN`) and confirm Inspector's `ecrImageInUseCount` / `ecrImageLastInUseAt` filters tie findings back to live workloads — AWS states this in-use mapping "is also supported on Fargate with Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS." For Lambda container-image agents check that same ECR configuration; for .zip agents check Inspector Lambda standard scanning and Lambda code scanning are both activated (standard is a prerequisite for code), that the function has been invoked or updated in the last 90 days and is `$LATEST`, and that it is not excluded by the `InspectorExclusion` / `InspectorCodeExclusion` tags. On Lambda MicroVMs this does not apply as a registry gate, because a MicroVM image is not an ECR artifact and Inspector has no MicroVM resource type — verify instead that CI scans the Dockerfile base image and lockfiles before the artifact is uploaded to S3.

controls.canonical_guidance: Check for enforcement that blocks pulling images from unapproved public registries into the AI workload environment. controls.canonical_question: Do containers running AI workloads run as non-root with the minimum OS-level privileges needed, rather than elevated/privileged mode by default?
controls.canonical_guidance: Verify pod/container security context disallows privileged mode and root execution unless explicitly justified. On ECS check the container definition for `user` (a non-root uid), `readonlyRootFilesystem: true` and `linuxParameters.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`, with Security Hub [ECS.20] and [ECS.5] as the detective backstop. On the Fargate launch type, privileged mode, host namespace sharing, `linuxParameters.devices`, `maxSwap`, `pidMode: host` and `networkMode: host` are all unavailable, so that class of hardening is moot rather than failing — note that [ECS.4] therefore passes vacuously on Fargate, since `privileged` cannot be set there at all, making it evidence of the launch type rather than of hardening. On ECS Managed Instances those knobs are settable again, so [ECS.4] carries real signal there. On Lambda this is satisfied by construction — "Lambda follows security best practices by defining a default Linux user with least-privileged permissions. This means that you don't need to specify a USER in your Dockerfile," on a filesystem where only `/tmp` is writable — so verify only that the agent image does not depend on root-owned files. On Lambda MicroVMs check `additionalOsCapabilities` is unset, since its only valid value is `["ALL"]`.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Apply the EKS Pod Security Standards restricted profile via Pod Security Admission namespace labels (enforce mode) so pods must set runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, privileged: false, and drop all Linux capabilities.

controls.required_proof: Patch cadence + drift-detection report
controls.canonical_question: Is the underlying host/node OS patched on a defined cadence, with a way to detect nodes that have fallen behind?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for automated patch management and drift detection for the compute layer hosting AI workloads. On ECS/Fargate, Lambda and Lambda MicroVMs this does not apply as written, because AWS owns and patches the host: "When using Fargate, customers are not responsible for securing the compute infrastructure that runs their containers," and Lambda workers are AWS-managed Nitro instances in an account customers cannot see, where "neither customers nor AWS operators can connect to a host running customer workloads" — so there is no AMI to pin, no node to cordon and no Inspector EC2 scanning target. Verify the obligations that do remain: for Fargate, that services run the `LATEST` platform version (Security Hub [ECS.10] / AWS Config `ecs-fargate-latest-platform-version`) and that `AWS_ECS_TASK_PATCHING_RETIREMENT` AWS Health events are handled; for Lambda .zip agents, that `UpdateRuntimeOn` is `Auto` (`GetRuntimeManagementConfig`); for Lambda MicroVMs, that images are rebuilt against the current `base-image-version` ahead of the DEPRECATED (60 days) / EXPIRING (30 days) / EXPIRED clock; and on every platform, that the customer's own image is rebuilt and redeployed on CVE publication — the one genuine customer patching duty everywhere. ECS Managed Instances sits in between: AWS provisions and patches the instance, but it is still a node, so confirm the patching cadence AWS applies is accepted rather than assuming a Fargate-style no-op.

controls.required_proof: Artifact signing/verification configuration
controls.canonical_question: Is there a signed/verified supply chain for the AI application code and dependencies deployed into these workloads?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm build artifacts are signed and verified at deploy time, with dependency provenance checked, not an unauthenticated pull-and-run. On ECS check for ECR managed signing (`ecr:PutSigningConfiguration` carrying a `signingConfiguration.rules[].signingProfileArn`) plus a verification gate at deploy — an ECS service `DeploymentLifecycleHook` at `PRE_SCALE_UP` whose Lambda runs the Notation CLI and returns `hookStatus: FAILED` to force rollback. Confirm the Lambda enforces rather than logs (in AWS's reference implementation this is the sample function's own failure-behavior switch, not an ECS API setting) and that `timeoutConfiguration.action` is `ROLLBACK` rather than `CONTINUE`; confirm too that no standalone `RunTask` agents exist, since every documented lifecycle stage is a service-deployment stage. On Lambda .zip agents check a code signing configuration is attached with `UntrustedArtifactOnDeployment` set to `Enforce` rather than the default `Warn`, that layers are signed by an allowed profile too, and that `lambda:CodeSigningConfigArn` is required org-wide. On Lambda container-image agents and Lambda MicroVMs there is no platform-side signature check, so verify signing happens in CI, verification happens in the pipeline before `UpdateFunctionCode` / `CreateMicrovmImage`, and the deployed reference is digest-pinned against an `IMMUTABLE` ECR repository.

controls.required_proof: Namespace/node isolation configuration
controls.canonical_question: Are compute resources for self-hosted agents isolated per workload/tenant at the node or namespace level, preventing one workload from accessing another's resources?
controls.canonical_guidance: Check for namespace/node-level isolation between distinct AI workloads, not a single shared, undifferentiated pool. On ECS/Fargate this is inherited and stronger than namespace isolation — "Each task running on Fargate has its own isolation boundary and does not share the underlying kernel, CPU resources, memory resources, or elastic network interface with another task." Establish the capacity type by two fields rather than one: the task definition's `requiresCompatibilities` should be `FARGATE`, and the service or task should resolve to Fargate capacity either through `launchType: FARGATE` or a `capacityProviderStrategy` naming only `FARGATE`/`FARGATE_SPOT`. A Managed Instances workload is identified by a `capacityProviderStrategy` with `launchType` omitted — you cannot request `MANAGED_INSTANCES` as a `launchType`, though `DescribeTasks` can return it — and on EC2, Managed Instances and ECS Anywhere "there is no task isolation," so containers can potentially reach credentials, environment variables and temporary files belonging to other tasks on the same instance. Verify each agent has its own `taskRoleArn` distinct from the execution role, and assess any sidecar tool-executor separately, since containers in one task share a network namespace and "can inter-communicate over localhost." On Lambda verify one function and one execution role per agent — "runtime environments are never reused across functions, function versions, or AWS accounts" — and that the handler scopes data to local variables and deletes `/tmp` files, since reuse within one function is possible. On Lambda MicroVMs verify one MicroVM per session or tenant and that tenant-specific material arrives via `runHookPayload`, not image-level `environmentVariables`, which are shared across every MicroVM run from that image version.

controls.canonical_question: Is there a tested ability to quickly isolate or terminate a specific compromised container/instance without taking down the entire cluster or fleet?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm a documented, exercised containment procedure exists for isolating a single compromised workload. On ECS confirm the runbook uses `ecs:StopTask` with a `reason` string, and that egress containment works by stripping rules from a security group the agent service owns exclusively — the deny-all-SG swap ported from EC2 fails because the task ENI is a fully managed ECS feature that your account "can't detach or modify." Confirm `ListTasks` is used to find sibling tasks running the same image, and that isolation (blocking inbound and outbound traffic, per GuardDuty's ECS remediation guidance) is preferred over termination so evidence survives. On Lambda confirm the runbook sets reserved concurrency to 0 and that a code or configuration update is used to force running execution environments to be replaced. On Lambda MicroVMs confirm containment is `TerminateMicrovm` or `SuspendMicrovm` plus halting token minting, and that in-guest evidence is captured over the shell before termination, because "network connectors are specified when you call run-microvm and cannot be changed while a MicroVM is running." On all of these, confirm the runbook does not call for a memory dump or disk image: the host is unreachable and there is no exec path into a Lambda execution environment at all.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Maintain a tested runbook to isolate a single compromised workload: apply a deny-all Kubernetes network policy to the affected pod, cordon and drain the node to stop new scheduling, and — if the underlying EC2 instance is suspected compromised — swap it to an isolation security group before terminating the node.

controls.canonical_question: For self-hosted models, are the model weights obtained from a verified source and integrity-checked before they are loaded, rather than pulled from a public hub and trusted on arrival?
controls.canonical_guidance: The weights are the asset in a self-hosted deployment, and the load path is where they are most exposed. Confirm two things: that the artifact came from a source you control or verified (a digest or signature checked against a recorded value, not just a repository name), and that it is checked immediately before load rather than only on download — a file staged on a shared volume can be replaced between the two. Distinct from AIR-SLF-CMP-01/02, which govern the container image; the weights are usually mounted or downloaded separately and never pass through image scanning. On ECS/Fargate verify the weights are mirrored into S3 or an EFS volume you control (with `transitEncryption: ENABLED` on the `efsVolumeConfiguration`) rather than pulled from a public hub at task start, that the digest re-check runs in the container entrypoint, and that the read permission sits on the task role rather than the execution role; Fargate ephemeral storage is already encrypted with an AES-256 key managed by Fargate and can take a customer-managed key at the cluster level, gated by the `ecs:fargate-ephemeral-storage-kms-key` condition key. On Lambda verify the digest check runs immediately before load in the handler or container entrypoint, sized against the 10 GB image limit or the `/tmp` ceiling (512–10,240 MB, encrypted at rest with an AWS-managed key). On Lambda MicroVMs verify weights are fetched or verified in the `/run` hook rather than baked into the snapshot, since build-time content is shared across every MicroVM run from the same image version. On all of these the IMDSv2 (`HttpTokens=required`) and Nitro Enclave / NitroTPM steps below do not apply, because there is no customer EC2 instance, no metadata service you configure and no attestation document — the substitute is least-privilege scoping of the single task or execution role plus egress restriction.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Treat model weights as a signed build artifact rather than a download. Mirror the model into an S3 bucket or ECR repository you control instead of pulling from a public hub at start-up, record the artifact's SHA256 digest at ingest, and re-verify that digest in the container entrypoint immediately before load so a substituted or truncated file fails closed rather than serving.

controls.canonical_question: Are secrets and credentials used by self-hosted agent workloads injected at runtime from a managed secrets store, rather than baked into images or environment files?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm secrets are pulled from a managed store at runtime; scan images/config for embedded credentials. On ECS (Fargate or ECS Managed Instances), confirm the container definition uses a `secrets` array of `valueFrom` ARNs (Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store) with a task execution role, and that Security Hub [ECS.8] / AWS Config `ecs-no-environment-secrets` is clean — that check fails when `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, or `ECS_ENGINE_AUTH_DATA` appear in `environment`, and it evaluates only the latest active task-definition revision. On Lambda MicroVMs, confirm per-session material arrives through `runHookPayload` and is resolved in the `/run` hook — image-level `environmentVariables` are set at image build time and injected into the snapshot, so every MicroVM launched from that image version shares them and nothing baked there is per-session or per-tenant.

controls.canonical_question: Is outbound network egress from self-hosted agent workloads restricted to an approved allow-list of destinations?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for an egress control (network policy, firewall, proxy) limiting outbound destinations rather than open egress. On ECS/Fargate, check the security group attached to the task's own ENI — `awsvpc` is the only network mode available to Fargate tasks, so a per-task egress firewall already exists and the question is whether its outbound rules are scoped. On ECS Managed Instances, check the task is in `awsvpc` mode rather than `host` mode: `awsvpc` gives each task its own ENI and security group, while in `host` mode tasks share the instance's network namespace and there is no per-task egress boundary to scope. On Lambda, check `VpcConfig.SubnetIds` / `SecurityGroupIds` are populated (AWS Config `lambda-inside-vpc`, Security Hub [Lambda.3]) — a function with no `VpcConfig` has unrestricted internet egress and no security group, NACL, or route table to constrain it. On Lambda MicroVMs, check `run-microvm` passes `--egress-network-connectors` pointing at a customer VPC egress connector rather than the Lambda-managed `INTERNET_EGRESS` connector, since public internet access is the documented default on the egress path.

controls.canonical_question: Is access to the underlying host or cluster control plane restricted and separately audited from application-level access to the AI workload?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm control-plane/host administrative access is distinct from and more tightly controlled than application access. On Fargate there is no host plane to inspect — AWS states neither customers nor AWS operators can connect to a host running a Fargate task — so verify instead that the ECS control plane (`ecs:RegisterTaskDefinition`, `ecs:UpdateService`) and interactive container access via ECS Exec are separately gated: `ecs:ExecuteCommand` held by a distinct role, `enableExecuteCommand` off unless needed, and the `ExecuteCommand` call itself in CloudTrail. On ECS Managed Instances the host plane is likewise unreachable by design — AWS lists no SSH access and no SSM Session Manager access as its responsibility — so ECS Exec and the ECS API are again the only planes to separate. On Lambda, verify the split between `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (the deploy plane, in CloudTrail management events by default) and `lambda:InvokeFunction` (the application plane, which requires opting `AWS::Lambda::Function` data events into CloudTrail before invocations are recorded at all). On Lambda MicroVMs, verify `lambda:CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken` is granted separately from `lambda:RunMicrovm`, that production MicroVMs are launched without the `SHELL_INGRESS` connector, and that CloudTrail data events are enabled for `AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage` — without that opt-in every `RunMicrovm` and every shell-token mint is unaudited.

controls.canonical_question: Is runtime behavior of self-hosted agent workloads (process activity, file access, network calls) monitored for anomalies, not just container-level health checks?
controls.canonical_guidance: Check for runtime security monitoring capturing process/file/network behavior, distinct from simple liveness/readiness probes. On ECS/Fargate this is a genuine yes: check GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is enabled with automated agent configuration for Fargate (Amazon ECS only) and that the ECS clusters runtime coverage shows the cluster healthy — then check the prerequisites that silently drop coverage: Linux only (Windows platform versions are not supported), platform version at least 1.4.0 or LATEST, a task execution role present with the ECR pull permissions, and — the prerequisite most often broken by AIR-SLF-RT-02's own egress allow-list — a network path from the task to the ECR repository hosting the GuardDuty agent (public IP, NAT gateway, or ECR interface endpoints) plus access to the S3 managed prefix list on port 443 where security groups restrict egress. Because a Fargate task is immutable, already-running tasks are not retrofitted — they must be stopped and started — and if the sidecar cannot launch healthy the task still runs, so read coverage statistics rather than treating enablement as coverage. On ECS Managed Instances this mechanism is unavailable: AWS states Runtime Monitoring is not supported for applications running on Amazon ECS Managed Instances, so the answer there is the lower tier below. On Lambda, check GuardDuty Lambda Protection is on (AWS Config `guardduty-lambda-protection-enabled`) together with Amazon Inspector Lambda standard and code scanning — and check the function does not set a customer-managed `KmsKeyArn`, because Inspector does not scan CMK-encrypted functions and that silently voids this half of the evidence. On Lambda MicroVMs, check VPC Flow Logs on the egress connector's ENIs, an execution role that actually forwards stdout/stderr to CloudWatch, and that `--logging` is not set to `{"disabled":{}}`, plus whatever in-guest instrumentation the customer added, because nothing managed watches process activity inside a MicroVM.

controls.canonical_guidance: Verify network policy (or security-group equivalent) restricts pod-to-pod/instance-to-instance reachability to declared dependencies. controls.canonical_question: Is secret and credential rotation for self-hosted agent workloads automated on a defined schedule, rather than performed manually and irregularly?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for scheduled, automated rotation with evidence of recent successful rotations, not a manual process that lapses. The rotation schedule is a Secrets Manager property and is checked the same way everywhere; what differs is whether the rotated value ever reaches the running agent, so check that second half per platform. On ECS (Fargate or ECS Managed Instances), injection happens only when the container starts — AWS states that if the secret is subsequently updated or rotated the container will not receive the updated value automatically — so confirm either a runtime fetch by the agent under its task role, or automation that calls `update-service --force-new-deployment` on rotation. On Lambda, confirm the function reads through the Parameters and Secrets extension at all rather than holding the value in a module-scope variable or a plaintext environment variable that never refreshes. On Lambda MicroVMs, confirm a `/resume` hook exists and re-fetches credentials — a suspended MicroVM is restored from a memory and disk checkpoint, so credentials established before suspend may have expired by the time it resumes, and a rotation schedule alone would pass a sandbox that never re-reads the secret.

controls.canonical_question: Can outbound network access for a specific compromised self-hosted agent workload be cut off immediately without disrupting unrelated workloads?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm a tested, granular egress-kill capability exists targeting a single workload, not an all-or-nothing network shutdown. On ECS/Fargate, confirm the runbook does not assume a security-group swap: the task ENI is a fully managed ECS feature your account cannot detach or modify, and changing a service's `networkConfiguration` launches new tasks rather than re-tagging running ones. The workable moves are stripping the rules from the security group the task already holds — so check each agent service has its own security group, otherwise rule-stripping hits every service sharing it — a deny-all NACL on the task's subnet (blast radius is the whole subnet), or `ecs:StopTask`. On ECS Managed Instances confirm the same and check `awsvpc` mode, since in `host` mode the only network lever is the instance's security group and it is shared by every task on that instance. On Lambda, confirm `put-function-concurrency --reserved-concurrent-executions 0` is the exercised off-switch, plus a security-group edit for VPC-attached functions. On Lambda MicroVMs, confirm the runbook is terminate-or-suspend rather than quarantine, because network connectors are specified at `run-microvm` and cannot be changed while a MicroVM is running.

controls.canonical_question: Is a serverless function that hosts agent or tool code invocable only by authenticated, authorized callers, rather than reachable by anyone holding its URL?
controls.canonical_guidance: Check the function's URL config and its resource-based policy, not just its execution role — the execution role governs what the function may do, this control governs who may run it. Run `aws lambda get-function-url-config` and confirm AuthType is AWS_IAM, not NONE: with NONE, Lambda auto-creates a resource policy whose Principal is "*", so any unauthenticated caller with the URL can invoke the function. Then run `aws lambda get-policy` and confirm no statement has Principal "*" without a narrowing condition. Two traps worth checking explicitly. First, deleting a function URL does NOT delete the resource-based policy Lambda created for it, so a function can show no URL config while still carrying a public-access statement — inspect the policy even when there is no URL. Second, when NONE is genuinely required (a browser-facing endpoint), confirm the policy includes the lambda:InvokedViaFunctionUrl condition, or the public grant extends to ordinary Invoke calls and not just the URL path. Also confirm the CORS allow-origin is not a bare wildcard where the endpoint is browser-facing.

controls.canonical_question: Are calls between self-hosted agents and the tools/APIs they invoke logged with enough detail to reconstruct an agent's full decision path?
controls.canonical_guidance: Verify logging captures each tool call, parameters, and result linked to the originating agent session. For Lambda MicroVMs check an execution role with logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents is supplied (without one, runtime stdout and stderr are silently not forwarded), that logging has not been disabled, and that CloudTrail data events are opted in on resources.type AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage so RunMicrovm and the token APIs are recorded.
