controls.required_proof: Delegation/handoff authorization configuration
controls.canonical_question: In multi-agent orchestration, is one agent prevented from impersonating or acting with another agent's authority without an explicit, checked handoff?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm agent-to-agent delegation requires an explicit, authorized handoff rather than implicit trust between co-located agents. STS source identity is platform-independent, so check it identically everywhere; what varies is the transport that carries the handoff. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) confirm each agent has its own task role and its own security group, and treat Service Connect TLS as transport encryption, not authorization — ECS has no NetworkPolicy analogue and matches on L3/L4 only. On Lambda inspect the function's resource-based policy for who may invoke it and confirm no Function URL uses AuthType NONE. For Lambda MicroVMs confirm one MicroVM per agent session, that CreateMicrovmAuthToken tokens are port-scoped and short-lived, and that lambda:CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken is denied where interactive shell is not needed.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Give each agent its own IAM role and require an explicit, authenticated handoff for delegation: a calling agent gets short-lived scoped credentials via sts:AssumeRole (never shared credentials), and inter-agent endpoints (e.g. API Gateway or an internal service) use IAM authorization so requests must be SigV4-signed with the caller's own identity.

src.t: Control access to an API with IAM permissions — SigV4-signed requests authorized against the caller's own identity

canonical_implementation_steps.do: To stop one agent acting with another's authority across the handoff, bind the originating identity into the delegated session with STS source identity (sts:SetSourceIdentity permission plus the sts:SourceIdentity trust-policy condition): once set it persists through role chaining, cannot be changed during the session, and appears as aws:SourceIdentity on every downstream request and in CloudTrail — so the target role's trust policy can require and pin the caller, and each handoff is authorized against least-privilege policies rather than implicit co-location trust.

src.t: Monitor and control actions taken with assumed roles — per-role attribution in CloudTrail and STS source identity

canonical_implementation_steps.do: That mechanism works unchanged on every host; only the transport-side authorization differs. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) give each agent its own task role and its own security group: each Fargate task gets its own ENI and security group, which is a genuine per-task firewall but matches on L3/L4 only, and on ECS Managed Instances or EC2 several tasks share an instance and can reach one another's credentials, so the checked handoff has to live in IAM/SigV4 at the inter-agent endpoint rather than in network placement.

src.t: Allocate a network interface for an Amazon ECS task — a per-task ENI with its own security group, and "Your account can't detach or modify the ENIs"

canonical_implementation_steps.do: ECS Service Connect with an AWS Private CA has ECS generate, rotate and distribute TLS 1.3 certificates between agent components, but scope the claim when you assess it: the seven-day maximum validity applies only when the private CA runs in short-lived mode — AWS's recommendation, because Service Connect does not support certificate revocation and relies on frequent rotation — whereas general-purpose mode allows any expiration date, communications fail if the rotation frequency exceeds seven days, and only traffic passing through the ECS agent is encrypted. Encryption is not an authorization layer either way.

src.t: Service Connect TLS — ECS-managed TLS 1.3 certificate generation and rotation, the seven-day validity applying to a short-lived-mode private CA, no certificate revocation support, and only ECS-agent traffic being encrypted

canonical_implementation_steps.do: On Lambda the resource-based policy is the inbound gate: grant lambda:InvokeFunction only to the specific calling agent's role, never a wildcard principal, and if a Function URL is used set AuthType to AWS_IAM, because with NONE Lambda performs no authentication and the function's resource-based policy has to grant public access for the URL to work at all.

src.t: Lambda resource-based policies — granting lambda:InvokeFunction to a named calling principal rather than a wildcard
Function URL authentication — with AuthType NONE Lambda performs no authentication and the resource-based policy must grant public access

canonical_implementation_steps.do: For Lambda MicroVMs the boundary is the MicroVM itself, since it holds exactly one executionRoleArn: run one MicroVM per agent session, mint short-lived port-scoped JWE tokens with CreateMicrovmAuthToken (the documented examples use a 30-minute expiration) with allowedPorts limited to the ports actually in use, so a request to any other port returns 403 Forbidden, and deny lambda:CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken separately so API access to a sandbox does not imply interactive shell — shell additionally requires the MicroVM to have been launched with the SHELL_INGRESS ingress connector, and simply not attaching that connector is the stronger control because create-microvm-shell-auth-token then fails with a ValidationException.

controls.required_proof: Scope-deviation detection configuration + example
controls.canonical_question: Is there monitoring that specifically detects an agent behaving outside its intended task scope (scope creep) before it causes broader impact?
controls.canonical_guidance: Look for behavioral monitoring tuned to detect deviation from expected task scope, not just error-rate or uptime metrics. On ECS on Fargate you also get a host-level behavioral tier: check GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is enabled with automated agent configuration for Fargate (Amazon ECS only) and that runtime coverage statistics show the security-agent sidecar present on every agent task. On ECS Managed Instances, Lambda and Lambda MicroVMs no such tier exists, so the custom-metric and log-based checks are the entire detection surface — verify the agent itself publishes the task-scope signals rather than treating the control as unanswerable. On Lambda additionally check an alarm on RecursiveInvocationsDropped and that GuardDuty Lambda Protection is on.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Publish custom CloudWatch metrics for task-scope signals (e.g. tool-call mix, invocation of tools outside the expected set, target resources touched) and apply CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms that learn each metric's normal baseline and fire when behavior falls outside the band.

controls.canonical_question: Is there a tested kill-switch that can pause or stop a specific self-hosted agent's orchestration without requiring a full platform redeploy?
controls.canonical_guidance: Confirm an operational control exists to halt one agent's execution quickly, exercised at least once, distinct from a full redeployment. On ECS check the rehearsed step stops one agent's service without disturbing siblings, and that each agent service has its own security group, because the task ENI is service-managed and your account cannot detach or modify it. On Lambda check put-function-concurrency --reserved-concurrent-executions 0 is the rehearsed off-switch. For Lambda MicroVMs check TerminateMicrovm and SuspendMicrovm are exercised per sandbox and that maximumDurationInSeconds is set on every launch.

controls.required_proof: Per-device certificate registration + an IoT policy showing thing policy variables and IsAttached, plus a clean Device Defender Audit
controls.canonical_question: Does each physical AI device carry its own unique cryptographic identity with an authorization policy scoped to that device, rather than a shared certificate or one fleet-wide policy granting broad topic access?
controls.canonical_guidance: Check three things, because a fleet can look well-governed and still share one credential. First, per-device identity: each thing has its own X.509 certificate (or its own private key in a hardware secure element) registered to exactly one thing, and provisioning does not ship a common certificate in the device image. Second, the policy is scoped by the device, not merely attached to it: look for AWS IoT Core thing policy variables (iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName, ThingTypeName, or Attributes[attributeName]) in the Resource or Condition, and specifically for the Bool condition iot:Connection.Thing.IsAttached = true, which is what stops a certificate being replayed for a thing it is not attached to. A policy granting iot:Publish or iot:Subscribe on topic/* is fleet-wide access however many certificates exist. Two traps: thing policy variables resolve ONLY over MQTT or MQTT-over-WebSocket, so a device using another transport gets no scoping from them; and where non-exclusive thing association is in use the same certificate may be attached to several things, in which case the MQTT client ID must exactly match the thing name or the variable resolves to the wrong thing. Third, no long-lived AWS credentials on the device: look for the AWS IoT credentials provider (iot:AssumeRoleWithCertificate against a role alias) rather than an access key in the firmware. Run AWS IoT Device Defender Audit and confirm the shared-certificate and permissive-policy checks are clean.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Give every device its own X.509 certificate, held in a hardware secure element or TPM where the platform offers one, and register it to exactly one thing with AttachThingPrincipal — never bake a common certificate into the device image, because recovering one device then yields the fleet.

controls.required_proof: Enumerated action space with parameter ranges + consequence classification + evidence the interlock is outside the agent's permissions
controls.canonical_question: Are the physical actions an AI agent can take bounded to an explicitly enumerated, safety-reviewed set, with hazardous or irreversible actuation gated on human approval and an interlock outside the agent's control path?
controls.canonical_guidance: This is the control with no AWS toggle, so verify it as a design property with three artifacts. First, an enumerated action space: a reviewed list of every physical action the agent may command, with the permitted parameter RANGE for each — a bound on consequence, not just on API surface. An IAM policy or Cedar policy that allows the actuation API without constraining its payload is not this control, because the harm lives in the parameter, not the call. Second, a consequence classification: which actions are reversible, which are not, and which can injure. Confirm the irreversible and hazardous ones require human approval at run time, and check the approval is enforced in the execution path rather than advisory in a prompt — a system prompt instructing the agent to ask first is not an enforcement point, because the agent is the thing you are bounding. Third, and most important: an interlock the agent cannot reach — a physical E-stop, a hardware limit, a rate or travel limiter, or an independent safety controller that holds even if the agent, its tools and its credentials are fully compromised. Confirm the agent has no permission that can disable, reconfigure or bypass it; if the interlock is reachable through any tool the agent holds, it is part of the agent, not a bound on it. Distinguish this from AIR-FND-GOV-09, which is the governance approval gate on high-impact actions generally; this control asks whether the physical action space itself is bounded.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Bound the action space in the tool layer, not in the prompt. Expose actuation to the agent only through a narrow tool contract that validates each parameter against a reviewed range and rejects anything outside it, so the agent cannot command a value no human approved — the tool, not the model, is the enforcement point.

src.t: The AWS AI Security Framework — agent permissions must include physical safety bounds

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Classify every action as reversible, irreversible or hazardous, and route the second two through an explicit human approval before execution: an AWS Step Functions human-approval task using the wait-for-callback pattern gives you an auditable gate outside the model's control, which a prompt instruction does not.

src.t: Step Functions human approval with the wait-for-callback pattern

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Keep a safety interlock entirely outside the agent's reach — a hardware E-stop, a mechanical or firmware travel and rate limit, or an independent safety controller — and verify by IAM and IoT policy review that no role, tool or credential the agent holds can disable, reconfigure or bypass it; assume the agent is compromised and check the bound still holds. Rehearse the failure: exercise the interlock and the approval path as part of the AI-specific incident response test, because an untested E-stop is a claim rather than a control.

src.t: The AWS AI Security Framework — physical AI is in scope for AI that acts

canonical_implementation_steps.do: On the device side, prefer commanding through a constrained interface (an AWS IoT job or a validated command topic whose handler enforces the same ranges) over granting the agent broad device control, and log every commanded action with its parameters and approval state so a physical incident can be reconstructed.

controls.required_proof: Build-pipeline signing or approved-artifact hash record + component recipe digests + bucket versioning/Object Lock configuration
controls.canonical_question: Is the model and agent code deployed to edge devices integrity-verified on the device before it runs, with provenance established before upload rather than inferred from the delivery channel?
controls.canonical_guidance: Separate the two halves, because the managed service covers only one of them. Transport integrity is largely inherited: when you create an AWS IoT Greengrass component, Greengrass calculates a cryptographic digest of each artifact and writes it into the component recipe, and the core device verifies each artifact against that digest on download — so tampering in the cloud or in transit is detected for you. What is NOT covered is provenance: AWS states you are responsible for securing software artifacts BEFORE you upload them to S3, so the digest proves the device got the bytes you uploaded, never that those bytes were the model your pipeline approved. So look upstream for the real control — a signing or attestation step in the build pipeline, a recorded hash of the approved model artifact, and a check that the uploaded object matches it. Confirm the artifact bucket resists silent replacement (versioning, and S3 Object Lock where the artifacts must not be overwritten or deleted at all), because overwriting the object and re-creating the component re-derives a valid digest for the wrong content. Also verify the runtime itself: Greengrass nucleus archives are signed from version 2.9.5 onward and can be checked with jarsigner -verify, which is a separate assurance from component artifact digests. Where the model is a container image, AWS Signer plus Notation gives signature verification rather than digest-only integrity — note the distinction, since an image digest establishes integrity but not authenticity.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Treat the Greengrass artifact digest as transport integrity and add provenance yourself, because that split is where edge deployments are actually attacked.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: Sign the model and agent artifacts in the build pipeline — AWS Signer, or a KMS asymmetric key with kms:Sign and kms:Verify — record the approved artifact's hash alongside the model-registry entry that approved it, and verify signature and hash before the artifact is uploaded to the component bucket.

canonical_implementation_steps.do: For container-packaged models use AWS Signer with Notation so the device or the deploying pipeline verifies a signature rather than only a digest, which establishes authenticity and not just integrity.
